approaches.name: Pediatric lateral approach to the distal fibula
approaches.corridor: Longitudinal exposure at posterior fibular border through the interval between peroneus tertius anteriorly and peroneus longus/brevis posteriorly

sources.title: Foot and ankle fractures during childhood: review

procedure_applications.condition: A displaced distal-fibular or lateral-malleolar fracture requires direct reduction and fixation

positioning.text: Position supine with a bump to rotate the fibula upward or lateral as needed, keeping AP, lateral, mortise, and oblique imaging available.

setup.text: Define the physis, fragment extent, implant position, and superficial-peroneal and sural-nerve danger zones before incision.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark fibular shaft and tip, distal-fibular physis, anterior and posterior fibular borders, superficial-peroneal-nerve course, and Achilles tendon.

incision.text: Use a longitudinal incision centered on fracture and biased to posterior fibular border so a lateral plate is not directly beneath the wound.

superficial_interval.text: Raise full-thickness flaps; identify superficial peroneal nerve with proximal/anterior extension and protect short saphenous vein and sural nerve posteriorly.

deep_interval.text: Develop the plane between peroneus tertius anteriorly and peroneus longus/brevis posteriorly, limiting periosteal elevation to the fracture and implant footprint.

layers.text: Skin, sensory-neurovascular plane, peroneal fascia, peroneus-tertius/peroneal interval, limited periosteum, then fibula.

structures_encountered.text: Superficial peroneal nerve, sural nerve, short saphenous vein, peroneus tertius, peroneus longus/brevis, physis, and fibula are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Superficial peroneal and sural nerves, short saphenous vein, peroneal tendons, distal-fibular physis/perichondral ring, fragment periosteum, and ankle cartilage are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Identify the superficial peroneal nerve proximally and sural nerve posteriorly before extending; minimize stripping around physis and fragment.

retraction_hazards.text: Use broad atraumatic retraction and avoid sustained pressure on sensory nerves or peroneal tendons.

exposure.text: Provides direct access to distal fibular shaft and lateral malleolar fragment with plate offset from incision.

limitations.text: Does not expose distal-tibial articular fragments and aggressive circumferential dissection threatens bone blood supply and physis.

extensions.text: Extend proximally or distally only after identifying the sensory nerve at risk and preserving tendon and physeal tissues.

indications.text: Use for displaced pediatric distal-fibular/lateral-malleolar fractures requiring open reduction, direct physeal alignment, or plate fixation.

relative_contraindications.text: Avoid open exposure for stable nondisplaced low-risk injuries and choose a posterior corridor when dominant posterior tibial pathology requires it.

implant_implications.text: Offset the plate from skin incision, respect physis and joint, and avoid screw trajectories that injure peroneal tendons or cross growth plate unnecessarily.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm length, rotation, mortise congruity, physeal alignment, and extra-articular implant position on AP, lateral, mortise, and oblique views.

closure.text: Restore peroneal fascia without nerve or tendon entrapment, confirm hemostasis, and close subcutaneous tissue and skin separately without plate prominence.

complications.text: Complications include physeal arrest, angular deformity, superficial-peroneal or sural neuropathy, tendon irritation, wound breakdown, infection, symptomatic hardware, and stiffness.

bailouts.text: Add a separate distal-tibial fragment-directed approach rather than circumferentially extending the fibular exposure across ankle.

questions.question: What is the deep interval?
questions.answer: Between peroneus tertius anteriorly and peroneus longus/brevis posteriorly.

questions.question: Why bias incision posteriorly?
questions.answer: So a lateral plate does not lie directly beneath incision.

questions.question: Which nerves bound proximal and posterior extension?
questions.answer: Superficial peroneal nerve proximally/anteriorly and sural nerve posteriorly.

approaches.name: Pediatric medial minimally invasive approach to the distal tibia
approaches.corridor: Short medial distal incision with submuscular/epiperiosteal plate advancement proximally while preserving physis and perichondral ring

sources.title: Minimally invasive medial plate osteosynthesis of high-energy pediatric tibia fractures
Modern management of paediatric tibial shaft fractures: evidence-based update

procedure_applications.condition: An unstable metaphyseal fracture requires bridge plating with maximal preservation of the injury-zone biology

positioning.text: Position supine on a radiolucent table with medial distal tibia accessible and full-length AP/lateral imaging available.

setup.text: Mark physis/perichondral ring, saphenous structures, fracture zone, plate path, and proximal screw sites; confirm indirect reduction strategy.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark medial malleolus, distal-tibial physis, medial tibial border, greater saphenous vein/nerve, and tibial shaft axis.

incision.text: Start just proximal to physis and extend proximally according to fracture/plate; begin at medial-malleolar tip only when plate must cross physis.

superficial_interval.text: Deepen through subcutaneous fat and retract greater saphenous vein and saphenous nerve anteriorly using a blunt retractor.

deep_interval.text: Avoid periosteal dissection at physis/perichondral ring and advance plate proximally in a submuscular, bone-hugging plane beneath intact injury-zone tissue.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous saphenous plane, preserved perichondral/periosteal layer, submuscular tunnel, then medial tibia.

structures_encountered.text: Greater saphenous vein, saphenous nerve, medial physis/perichondral ring, periosteum, and medial tibia are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Saphenous nerve/vein, distal-tibial physis and perichondral ring, periosteal blood supply, skin over plate, and posterior structures with off-bone tunneling are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Do not dissect periosteum at physis or injure perichondral ring; keep plate on bone and visualize each percutaneous screw trajectory.

retraction_hazards.text: Retract saphenous structures bluntly anterior and avoid forceful tunneling that perforates skin, strips periosteum, or enters fracture.

exposure.text: Permits submuscular bridge plating while preserving soft tissue and blood supply within metaphyseal injury zone.

limitations.text: Does not directly expose articular comminution and relies on imaging and indirect reduction to prevent malalignment.

extensions.text: Use separate proximal stab incisions for screws or an anterolateral tunnel when medial soft tissue is compromised.

indications.text: Use for selected unstable pediatric distal-tibial metaphyseal or high-energy tibial fractures suited to bridge plating.

relative_contraindications.text: Choose direct reduction for displaced articular/physeal incongruity and another fixation method when plate crosses critical physis unnecessarily or medial skin is unsafe.

implant_implications.text: Choose pediatric-appropriate plate length and contour, minimize physeal crossings, and position screws through targeted incisions away from physis and neurovascular structures.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Use full-length AP/lateral and ankle views to verify length, rotation, coronal/sagittal alignment, physis, plate position, and screw containment.

closure.text: Ensure saphenous structures are free and plate is not prominent beneath skin, then close each incision in layers without tension.

complications.text: Complications include physeal injury, malalignment, saphenous neuritis, skin/plate irritation, infection, delayed union/nonunion, and implant removal.

bailouts.text: Add a limited direct-reduction window or change fixation when indirect maneuvers cannot restore acceptable length, rotation, and alignment.

questions.question: Which structures are retracted anteriorly?
questions.answer: Greater saphenous vein and saphenous nerve.

questions.question: Which growth structure must not be dissected?
questions.answer: The perichondral ring at distal tibial physis.

questions.question: When does incision begin at malleolar tip?
questions.answer: When fracture configuration requires plate to cross physis.

approaches.name: Pediatric posterolateral approach to the distal tibia
approaches.corridor: Just lateral to Achilles, through medial border of peroneal muscles with peroneals retracted laterally to expose posterior tibia

sources.title: Foot and ankle fractures during childhood: review

procedure_applications.condition: A displaced posterior or posterolateral distal-tibial fragment requires direct reduction
Posterior distal-fibular access is required with posterior tibial exposure

positioning.text: Position prone or lateral with posterior ankle accessible and fluoroscopy preconfigured for AP, lateral, mortise, and oblique views.

setup.text: Use CT to confirm posterior fragment morphology, mark physis and sural nerve course, and plan whether tibia alone or tibia and fibula require exposure.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark lateral Achilles border, fibular tip, distal-tibial and fibular physes, sural-nerve course, and posterior joint line.

incision.text: Make a longitudinal incision approximately 0.5 cm lateral and parallel to lateral Achilles border, centered on posterior pathology.

superficial_interval.text: Raise full-thickness flaps, identify/protect sural nerve, and expose peroneal muscles.

deep_interval.text: Develop medial border of peroneal muscles and retract them laterally to expose posterior and posterolateral distal-tibial fragments.

layers.text: Skin, sural-nerve plane, peroneal fascia, medial peroneal border, posterior periosteum/capsule, then posterior distal tibia.

structures_encountered.text: Sural nerve, short saphenous vein, peroneal muscles/tendons, Achilles tendon border, distal physes, posterior capsule, and posterior fragments are encountered.

structures_at_risk.text: Sural nerve, short saphenous vein, peroneal tendons, posterior tibial neurovascular structures medially, physes/perichondral rings, periosteum, and cartilage are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Identify sural nerve before proximal extension and keep dissection immediately along medial peroneal border without drifting toward posteromedial bundle.

retraction_hazards.text: Retract peroneals gently laterally and avoid forceful medial retraction or circumferential fragment/physeal stripping.

exposure.text: Provides direct access to posterior and posterolateral distal-tibial fragments and can reach posterior distal fibula.

limitations.text: Anterior and medial articular fragments are not directly visualized and posterior pediatric structures constrain medial extension.

extensions.text: Extend along either side of identified sural nerve or add a separate fragment-directed anterior/medial incision when necessary.

indications.text: Use for displaced posterior/posterolateral distal-tibial physeal or transitional fragments requiring direct reduction and buttress fixation.

relative_contraindications.text: Choose anterior or medial exposure for dominant nonposterior pathology or when posterior skin/positioning is unsafe.

implant_implications.text: Use fragment-specific posterior fixation that avoids physis, joint, peroneal tendons, and posteromedial bundle; maintain enough soft-tissue coverage over hardware.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Confirm posterior reduction, physeal alignment, mortise congruity, and implant containment on AP, lateral, mortise, and oblique views.

closure.text: Return peroneal muscles anatomically, close deep fascia only without tension, ensure sural nerve is free, and close skin in layers.

complications.text: Complications include sural neuropathy, peroneal-tendon irritation, wound problems, physeal arrest, angular deformity, infection, stiffness, and post-traumatic arthritis.

bailouts.text: Add a separate fragment-directed incision when anterior/medial reduction cannot be confirmed rather than extending across protected posterior structures.

questions.question: Where is incision relative to Achilles?
questions.answer: About 0.5 cm lateral and parallel to lateral Achilles border.
